newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan court frees woman to join husband.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan court frees woman to join husband.

text.p: A Pakistani court freed a woman to join her husband on Monday, dismissing her Moslem fundamentalist father's petition that their marriage was invalid because it had taken place without his permission.
"I am so glad to have got justice. I deserved it," Saima Waheed, a 22-year-old business administration student, told Reuters at a women's shelter in Lahore after the decision.
"For 11 months I have been under a sort of house arrest. I wasn't allowed to meet anyone except my blood relations, who constantly threatened and harassed me," she said.
The case tested whether women have legal autonomy in Islamic Pakistan and touched on the precedence of Islamic precepts in Pakistani law and how strictly they should be interpreted.
A three-judge bench of the Lahore High Court earlier ruled 2-1 that a marriage conducted without the consent of a wali (guardian) was not invalid, as contended by Saima's father.
His argument that in Islam a woman can only marry with her father's permission, even if she is of age, produced what has been seen as a test case for women's rights in the country.
"It is the most wonderful day of my life," said Saima's husband, college lecturer Arshad Ahmad, at the court.
"We have gone through a great ordeal that was spread over 11 months. But now I can join hands with my wife once again. I am extremely happy."
Saima did not say, apparently for security reasons, exactly when she would leave the women's shelter where she has been staying under a court order, but said she would rejoin her husband soon.
"I want to go back to my husband and complete my education," she said, but added that her troubles might not be over.

"My parents are very influential and very rich. They are not going to give up on me yet. They will take me further in the courts," she said. "But I am ready. I have courage, I have Arshad's love, I have everything."
Saima's father Abdul Waheed Ropri and his followers left the court-room silently after the decision, on which Ropri refused to comment. "There's no use in talking now," he said.
Legal sources said Ropri, a member of the militant Sunni Moslem Ahle Hadith organisation, could appeal to the Supreme Court against the dismissal of his habeas corpus petition.
"It's a historic decision for the women of Pakistan," said Asma Jahangir, Saima's lawyer and chairperson of the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP).
Jahangir said she was sure Saima's parents would appeal to the Supreme Court.

"The court is worried that young people should not defy their parents, but at the same time they cannot curb the rights of young people, so they have tried to take a very balanced approach towards that," she said of Monday's ruling.
The case was one of the most controversial faced by the Lahore High court since a 1994 trial of three Christians accused of blaspheming the Prophet Mohammed.
Jahangir also defended the three Christians, one of whom was shot dead outside the Lahore High Court building and two of whom fled to Germany after their acquittal in 1995.
